subtopics.name: Upper GI disorders and GI bleeding

questions.stem: Twenty minutes into a laparoscopic cholecystectomy under general anesthesia with sevoflurane and succinylcholine, a 26-year-old client's end-tidal CO2 rises from 38 to 72 mm Hg despite increased ventilation. Heart rate is 142/min with ectopic beats, the jaw and limbs are rigid, and temperature has risen from 37.0 °C to 39.4 °C (103 °F). Complete the diagram by placing the condition the client is most likely experiencing, 2 actions the nurse should take, and 2 parameters the nurse should monitor.

actions.text: Stop the triggering anesthetic and prepare IV dantrolene
Start active cooling, such as cold IV saline and ice packs to the groin and axillae
Give acetaminophen through the nasogastric tube for the fever
Give another dose of succinylcholine to relax the rigid muscles
Warm the IV fluids to prevent shivering during the case

rationale.correct: Malignant hyperthermia: rising end-tidal CO2, rigidity, tachycardia and fever after volatile anesthetics or succinylcholine. Stop the trigger, give dantrolene, cool, and monitor temperature, CO2 and potassium.

perOption.c1: A rapid rise in end-tidal CO2, tachycardia, muscle rigidity and rising temperature after a volatile anesthetic and succinylcholine is malignant hyperthermia.
perOption.c2: Sepsis does not cause sudden rigidity and a sharp rise in CO2 during anesthesia.
perOption.c3: Thyroid storm causes fever and tachycardia but not rigidity and an abrupt rise in end-tidal CO2.
perOption.c4: NMS follows antipsychotics and develops over days, not minutes into anesthesia.
perOption.a1: Removing the trigger and giving dantrolene stops the runaway muscle metabolism.
perOption.a2: Cooling limits organ damage from hyperthermia.
perOption.a3: The heat comes from muscle metabolism, not the brain's set point; antipyretics do not work.
perOption.a4: Succinylcholine is a trigger and would worsen the crisis.
perOption.a5: Warming adds heat to a client who is already hyperthermic.
perOption.p1: Shows whether cooling and dantrolene are working; cooling stops at about 38 °C to avoid overshoot.
perOption.p2: Falling end-tidal CO2 shows metabolism is slowing; potassium rises with muscle breakdown and can cause dysrhythmias.
perOption.p3: Glucose may change but is not the key guide to the crisis.
perOption.p4: Bowel function is not relevant to the crisis.
perOption.p5: Pupil size does not guide treatment of malignant hyperthermia.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)

questions.stem: A client had a lumbar puncture yesterday. Today the client reports a severe headache that is much worse when sitting up and eases when lying flat. Vital signs and neurological checks are normal, and there is no fever or neck stiffness. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Keep the client sitting upright so that the spinal fluid can drain away from the head and the pain eases
Encourage the client to lie flat, increase fluids and report the headache to the provider
Prepare the client for an emergency CT scan of the head to rule out a bleed
Restrict oral fluids so that the pressure in the spinal canal does not rise further

rationale.correct: Post-dural puncture headache worsens upright and eases lying flat; treat with rest flat, fluids, caffeine and, if needed, an epidural blood patch.

perOption.a: Sitting up worsens a post-dural puncture headache.
perOption.b: A positional headache after lumbar puncture is from a spinal fluid leak; lying flat, fluids and caffeine help, and a blood patch may be needed.
perOption.c: With normal neurological checks and a classic positional pattern, emergency imaging is not the first step.
perOption.d: Fluids help the body replace spinal fluid; restricting them worsens the headache.

questions.stem: A client returned to the unit 1 hour ago after a bronchoscopy with topical throat anesthesia and moderate sedation. The client is awake and asks for a drink of water. What should the nurse do first?

options.text: Give small sips of water and watch for coughing as the client swallows them
Check that the client's gag and swallow reflexes have returned
Give ice chips, since they melt slowly and are safer than plain water
Tell the client to wait 24 hours before eating or drinking anything

rationale.correct: After bronchoscopy or endoscopy with throat anesthesia, keep the client NPO until the gag and swallow reflexes return.

perOption.a: Fluids are not offered until the gag reflex has returned.
perOption.b: Topical anesthesia blunts the gag reflex; giving fluids before it returns risks aspiration.
perOption.c: Ice chips are still fluid and carry the same risk before the gag reflex returns.
perOption.d: The gag reflex usually returns within a few hours, so a 24-hour wait is not needed.

questions.stem: A client is scheduled for an exercise stress test tomorrow morning to evaluate chest pain. Which instruction should the nurse give the client?

options.text: Avoid coffee, tea, cola and chocolate for 24 hours before the test
Eat a large, high-carbohydrate breakfast to have energy for the exercise
Wear dress shoes and a button-down shirt so the electrodes stay in place
Take an extra dose of the beta-blocker to keep the heart rate low during the test

rationale.correct: Before a stress test: no caffeine for about 24 hours, a light meal or fasting as directed, comfortable shoes and clothes, and follow instructions about holding heart rate-slowing drugs.

perOption.a: Caffeine can affect heart rate and interfere with the test, especially if a drug stress agent is needed.
perOption.b: A light meal or fasting for a few hours is usually advised; a large meal can cause discomfort and affect results.
perOption.c: Comfortable clothes and walking shoes are needed for the treadmill.
perOption.d: Beta-blockers are often held before the test as prescribed, because they stop the heart rate from rising.

questions.stem: The nurse in a cardiac step-down unit receives four laboratory results. Which result should the nurse report to the provider first?

options.text: Hemoglobin A1C of 8.2% in a client with type 2 diabetes who was admitted for a foot wound
Potassium of 3.4 mEq/L in a client taking furosemide who has no ECG changes and no muscle weakness
Troponin I of 2.1 ng/mL in a client who reports pressure in the chest that started 1 hour ago
Total cholesterol of 262 mg/dL in a client with hypertension who is being discharged today

rationale.correct: Report results that point to an acute, life-threatening process first; a rising troponin with chest pain suggests MI.

perOption.a: A high A1C shows poor long-term glucose control but is not an emergency.
perOption.b: Mild hypokalemia needs replacement but is less urgent.
perOption.c: A high troponin with ongoing chest pressure suggests a myocardial infarction that needs urgent treatment.
perOption.d: High cholesterol is a long-term risk factor that can be addressed in follow-up.

questions.stem: A client in labor received an epidural for pain relief 20 minutes ago. For each finding, indicate whether it is expected or should be reported right away.

rows.text: Warmth and numbness of both legs
Blood pressure 82/48 mm Hg from a baseline of 124/76
Numbness rising to the level of the nipples with trouble breathing
Pain score falling from 8 to 2 of 10

rationale.correct: Expected: leg numbness, pain relief, mild itching. Report at once: hypotension and a rising block with breathing trouble.

perOption.r1:c1: Sensory and some motor block of the legs is expected with an epidural.
perOption.r2:c1: A large drop in blood pressure reduces blood flow to the placenta.
perOption.r2:c2: Hypotension is a common epidural complication that needs prompt treatment.
perOption.r3:c1: A high block can affect breathing muscles.
perOption.r3:c2: This is a high spinal block and needs urgent help.
perOption.r4:c2: This shows the epidural is working.
perOption.r5:c1: Itching is a common side effect of epidural opioids.
perOption.r5:c2: It is usually mild and treatable.

questions.stem: A client with suspected sepsis has a prescription for IV piperacillin-tazobactam now and two sets of blood cultures. The antibiotic has just arrived from the pharmacy, and the cultures have not yet been drawn. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Start the antibiotic now and draw the blood cultures when the infusion is finished
Draw both sets of blood cultures, then start the antibiotic within the first hour
Wait for the culture results before starting any antibiotic, to choose the right one
Draw one set of cultures from the existing IV line to save time, then start the drug

rationale.correct: In sepsis, draw blood cultures before antibiotics, but do not delay antibiotics beyond the first hour.

perOption.a: Antibiotics given before cultures can sterilize the blood and hide the organism.
perOption.b: Cultures are drawn first so the organism can be identified, without delaying antibiotics beyond the first hour.
perOption.c: Results take days; delaying antibiotics in sepsis increases mortality.
perOption.d: Cultures from an existing line are often contaminated; separate venipunctures are preferred.

questions.stem: A client is scheduled for an MRI of the brain. Which findings should the nurse report to the radiology team before the scan? Select all that apply.

options.text: The client has a cardiac pacemaker placed 5 years ago
The client says, "I panic in small, closed spaces."
The client is wearing a transdermal nicotine patch
The client had a silver amalgam dental filling placed last year
The client worked as a welder for 20 years
The client reports an allergy to penicillin that causes a rash

rationale.correct: Before MRI, screen for implanted devices, metal fragments, medication patches and claustrophobia.

perOption.a: Many pacemakers are not MRI-safe; the device type must be checked.
perOption.b: Claustrophobia may need an open MRI or sedation.
perOption.c: Some patches contain metal that can heat up and burn the skin.
perOption.d: Dental fillings do not prevent an MRI.
perOption.e: Metal fragments in the eyes or body can move in the magnet; screening may be needed.
perOption.f: A penicillin allergy does not affect MRI safety.

questions.stem: A client had a cardiac catheterization through the right radial artery 2 hours ago, and a compression band is on the wrist. Which finding requires the nurse to act first?

options.text: Mild soreness at the puncture site that the client rates 2 of 10
A small amount of dried blood under the edge of the band
The right hand is cool and pale, with capillary refill of 5 seconds
The client asks to use the right hand to cut food and eat lunch from the meal tray

rationale.correct: After radial access, check circulation to the hand often; a cool, pale hand with slow capillary refill needs immediate action.

perOption.a: Mild soreness is expected after radial access.
perOption.b: A small amount of dried blood is common; the nurse checks it is not growing.
perOption.c: A cool, pale hand with slow refill suggests the band is too tight or the artery is blocked, threatening blood flow to the hand.
perOption.d: The client should limit use of the wrist, but this is a teaching issue, not an emergency.

questions.stem: A client with a complete spinal cord injury at T4 from 6 months ago is in a rehabilitation unit. The client suddenly reports a pounding headache and blurred vision. Blood pressure is 214/118 mm Hg (baseline 98/60) and heart rate is 48/min. The face is flushed and sweaty, and the skin below the chest is pale and cool. The urinary catheter bag has not drained for 3 hours. Complete the diagram by placing the condition the client is most likely experiencing, 2 actions the nurse should take, and 2 parameters the nurse should monitor.

actions.text: Sit the client upright and lower the legs
Check the catheter for kinks or blockage and drain the bladder
Lay the client flat with the legs raised
Give a sedative and recheck the blood pressure in 1 hour
Apply tight elastic stockings to both legs

parameters.text: Blood glucose before meals and at bedtime
Bowel sounds in each of the four quadrants

rationale.correct: Autonomic dysreflexia in injuries at T6 or above: sit the client up, loosen clothing, find and remove the trigger (bladder, bowel, skin) and monitor blood pressure closely.

perOption.c1: Severe hypertension, bradycardia, headache and flushing above the injury in a client with an injury at T6 or above, with a blocked catheter, is autonomic dysreflexia.
perOption.c2: The client has a low baseline pressure and no history of hypertension; the trigger and pattern point to dysreflexia.
perOption.c3: Spinal shock occurs soon after injury and causes low blood pressure and flaccid paralysis.
perOption.c4: Headache and hypertension can occur, but flushing above the injury with a blocked catheter fits dysreflexia.
perOption.a1: Sitting up lowers blood pressure by pooling blood in the legs.
perOption.a2: Removing the trigger, most often a full bladder, usually resolves the episode.
perOption.a3: Lying flat raises blood pressure further.
perOption.a4: The emergency needs the trigger found now; waiting risks stroke or seizure.
perOption.a5: Tight clothing and stockings are possible triggers and should be loosened.
perOption.p1: Blood pressure shows whether removing the trigger is working or whether medication is needed.
perOption.p2: Restored drainage confirms the trigger has been removed.
perOption.p3: Glucose is not related to dysreflexia.
perOption.p4: Bowel sounds do not show response, though constipation can be a trigger.
perOption.p5: Sodium does not guide this emergency.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)

questions.stem: A client with small cell lung cancer has a serum sodium of 121 mEq/L, serum osmolality of 252 mOsm/kg and concentrated urine. The client is becoming confused. The provider diagnoses the syndrome of inappropriate antidiuretic hormone (SIADH). Which intervention should the nurse expect?

options.text: Encourage the client to drink at least 3 L of water a day
Restrict fluids and put seizure precautions in place
Give a continuous infusion of 5% dextrose in water
Give desmopressin to control the amount of urine produced

rationale.correct: SIADH: too much ADH causes water retention and dilutional hyponatremia. Restrict fluids, monitor sodium and neurological status and use seizure precautions.

perOption.a: Extra free water lowers sodium further.
perOption.b: SIADH causes water retention; fluid restriction raises sodium, and very low sodium can cause seizures.
perOption.c: D5W acts as free water and worsens hyponatremia.
perOption.d: Desmopressin is an antidiuretic hormone and would worsen SIADH.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)

questions.stem: A client with stable angina takes sublingual nitroglycerin 0.4 mg as needed. Which instruction should the nurse give for an episode of chest pain?

options.text: Take one tablet, and if the pain is no better after 5 minutes, call 911
Take up to three tablets at once to stop the chest pain quickly
Swallow the tablet whole with a full glass of water so that it starts working faster
Wait 30 minutes after the first tablet before taking another dose

rationale.correct: Nitroglycerin: one tablet under the tongue; if not better in 5 minutes, call 911, and repeat every 5 minutes up to three doses while sitting down.

perOption.a: Current guidance is to call emergency services if pain is not improved 5 minutes after the first dose.
perOption.b: Taking several tablets at once can cause severe hypotension.
perOption.c: Sublingual nitroglycerin dissolves under the tongue; swallowing it greatly reduces its effect.
perOption.d: Doses are repeated every 5 minutes, up to three, while emergency help is on the way.

questions.stem: A client taking phenytoin 300 mg daily for a seizure disorder recently started fluconazole for a fungal infection. The client now has an unsteady gait, slurred speech and jerky eye movements when looking to the side. Which finding should the nurse expect when reviewing the laboratory results?

options.text: A phenytoin level below the therapeutic range of 10 to 20 mcg/mL
A phenytoin level of 28 mcg/mL, above the therapeutic range
A serum sodium level of 128 mEq/L from the antifungal drug
A blood glucose level of 52 mg/dL from the interaction between the drugs

rationale.correct: Phenytoin toxicity causes nystagmus, ataxia and slurred speech; drugs that slow its metabolism, such as fluconazole, raise levels.

perOption.a: A low level would cause seizures, not ataxia and nystagmus.
perOption.b: Fluconazole slows phenytoin metabolism; nystagmus, ataxia and slurred speech are signs of phenytoin toxicity.
perOption.c: Fluconazole does not typically cause hyponatremia, and the signs fit phenytoin toxicity.
perOption.d: Low glucose can cause confusion but not this pattern of nystagmus and ataxia.

references: Nursing pharmacology texts (e.g. Lehne; McCuistion) and the drug's prescribing information

questions.stem: Review the 2230 findings. Highlight the findings that require immediate follow-up.

segments.text: vomited a large amount of bright red blood

rationale.correct: Hematemesis with falling blood pressure, tachycardia and low hemoglobin means active hemorrhage with shock.

perOption.s2: Large-volume hematemesis signals active upper GI bleeding.
perOption.s4: A chronic sign of cirrhosis, not an acute concern.
perOption.s6: Falling blood pressure shows shock from blood loss.
perOption.s8: Rising heart rate is compensation for hypovolemia.
perOption.s10: A low hemoglobin confirms major blood loss.

questions.educationalObjective: Recognize cues of upper GI hemorrhage.

questions.stem: Complete the sentence based on the client's data.

content.template: The bleeding is most likely from {{b1}}, which develop because of {{b2}}.

options.text: esophageal varices
a duodenal ulcer
a Mallory-Weiss tear
portal hypertension from scarring of the liver
low platelets from the spleen
high ammonia levels

rationale.correct: Cirrhosis causes portal hypertension, which leads to esophageal varices that can rupture and bleed massively.

perOption.b1:a: Varices are the classic cause of massive bright red hematemesis in cirrhosis.
perOption.b1:b: Ulcers can bleed, but the history of cirrhosis makes varices most likely.
perOption.b1:c: Tears follow forceful vomiting and are usually smaller bleeds.
perOption.b2:a: Scarring raises pressure in the portal vein, which forces blood into fragile collateral veins.
perOption.b2:b: Low platelets worsen bleeding but do not create varices.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)

questions.educationalObjective: Analyze the cause of variceal bleeding.

questions.stem: Complete the diagram by placing the condition the client is most likely experiencing, 2 actions the nurse should take, and 2 parameters the nurse should monitor.

condition.text: Hypovolemic shock from ruptured esophageal varices

actions.text: Give blood products and IV fluids as prescribed through the large-bore IVs
Insert a nasogastric tube and irrigate with iced saline
Place the client flat on the back to raise the blood pressure
Give a dose of oral propranolol now for the heart rate

parameters.text: Hemoglobin and signs of ongoing bleeding
Body weight measured once a week
Burning or pain when the client urinates

rationale.correct: Variceal hemorrhage: resuscitate with blood and fluids, give octreotide and antibiotics, protect the airway and prepare for endoscopic banding.

perOption.c1: Massive hematemesis with hypotension, tachycardia and a low hemoglobin in cirrhosis is variceal hemorrhage with shock.
perOption.c2: Ammonia is high, but the life threat right now is blood loss.
perOption.c3: Withdrawal may come later, but bleeding is the current emergency.
perOption.c4: SBP causes fever and abdominal pain, not hematemesis.
perOption.a1: Restoring volume and red cells treats shock.
perOption.a2: Octreotide lowers portal pressure and slows variceal bleeding.
perOption.a3: Iced saline lavage is not recommended and can injure tissue.
perOption.a4: Lying flat increases aspiration risk in a client who is vomiting blood.
perOption.a5: Beta-blockers prevent future bleeds; in acute shock they lower blood pressure further.

questions.stem: Which actions should the nurse anticipate for this client in the next hour? Select all that apply.

options.text: Prepare the client for an urgent endoscopy with banding
Raise the head of the bed and keep suction ready at the bedside
Give a prophylactic IV antibiotic such as ceftriaxone as prescribed
Encourage the client to drink clear fluids to replace lost volume
Give lactulose by mouth now for the high ammonia
Prepare for possible intubation to protect the airway

rationale.correct: Variceal bleeding care: airway protection, NPO, endoscopic banding, antibiotics and resuscitation.

perOption.a: Endoscopic band ligation is the main treatment to stop variceal bleeding.
perOption.b: Protects the airway from aspiration of blood.
perOption.c: Antibiotics reduce infection and death in clients with cirrhosis and GI bleeding.
perOption.d: The client should be NPO for endoscopy and is at aspiration risk.
perOption.e: Lactulose may be needed, but not by mouth while the client is vomiting blood and awaiting endoscopy.
perOption.f: Clients with massive hematemesis and agitation are often intubated before endoscopy.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)

questions.stem: The provider prescribes an octreotide infusion. Which effect of the drug should the nurse explain to the client's family?

options.text: It narrows the blood vessels that feed the varices and lowers pressure in the portal vein
It helps the blood clot faster by raising the number of platelets circulating in the bloodstream
It neutralizes the stomach acid that is eroding the thin walls of the swollen veins in the esophagus
It removes ammonia from the bowel to prevent confusion from liver failure

rationale.correct: Octreotide lowers portal pressure by reducing splanchnic blood flow and is used with endoscopic therapy for variceal bleeding.

perOption.a: Octreotide reduces splanchnic blood flow and portal pressure, which slows variceal bleeding.
perOption.c: Acid reducers such as pantoprazole do that; octreotide works on blood flow.

references: Nursing pharmacology texts (e.g. Lehne; McCuistion) and the drug's prescribing information

questions.stem: The next morning, after banding and 3 units of packed red blood cells, the nurse reviews the client's data. For each finding, indicate whether it shows improvement or needs follow-up.

rows.text: Blood pressure 112/68 mm Hg and heart rate 92/min
New confusion and a flapping tremor of the hands
No further vomiting of blood overnight

rationale.correct: Stable hemoglobin and vital signs show bleeding is controlled; new confusion and asterixis show hepatic encephalopathy, which blood in the gut can trigger.

perOption.r1:c1: Hemoglobin has risen after transfusion and has stayed stable.
perOption.r1:c2: This shows bleeding has been controlled.
perOption.r2:c1: Vital signs are close to normal.
perOption.r3:c1: Asterixis and confusion suggest hepatic encephalopathy, often triggered by GI bleeding.
perOption.r4:c1: No new hematemesis suggests the bands are holding.

perOption.r3: Low-grade fever is common in RSV and is not the priority.
perOption.r4: Too few wet diapers shows dehydration from poor feeding.
perOption.r5: Expected in bronchiolitis; managed with suctioning.

questions.stem: Complete the sentence based on the infant's data.

content.template: The infant has {{b1}} and is at high risk because of {{b2}}.

options.text: bronchiolitis with increasing respiratory distress
croup with upper airway obstruction
asthma
young age and premature birth
the low-grade fever
being breastfed

rationale.correct: Young age, prematurity, heart and lung disease and immune problems raise the risk of severe bronchiolitis.

perOption.b1:a: RSV infection with retractions, flaring, tachypnea and falling SpO2 is worsening bronchiolitis.
perOption.b1:b: Croup causes a barking cough and stridor, not wheezes and crackles in both lungs.
perOption.b1:c: Asthma is not diagnosed at 3 months, and the RSV panel explains the picture.
perOption.b2:a: Infants under 3 months and those born preterm have the highest risk of severe RSV disease.
perOption.b2:b: Fever does not drive the risk of severe disease.
perOption.b2:c: Breastfeeding is protective, not a risk factor.

questions.stem: For each potential problem, indicate whether the infant is at high or low immediate risk based on the current data.

rationale.correct: Young infants with RSV are at risk of respiratory failure, dehydration and apnea.

perOption.r1:c1: Worsening tachypnea and falling SpO2 point to tiring.
perOption.r1:c2: Falling SpO2 makes this risk high.
perOption.r2:c1: Poor feeding and few wet diapers show fluid deficit.
perOption.r2:c2: Low urine output makes this risk high.
perOption.r3:c1: Young preterm infants with RSV are at risk of apnea.
perOption.r3:c2: Age and prematurity make this risk high.
perOption.r4:c1: Febrile seizures usually occur from 6 months to 5 years.
perOption.r4:c2: At 3 months with a low-grade fever, this risk is low.

questions.educationalObjective: Prioritize risks in an infant with bronchiolitis.

questions.stem: Which interventions should the nurse anticipate for the infant? Select all that apply.

options.text: Suction the nose gently before feedings and as needed
Give humidified oxygen to keep the SpO2 at or above 90%
Give a nebulized bronchodilator every 4 hours as standard care
Start IV or nasogastric fluids if the infant cannot feed safely
Give an oral corticosteroid to reduce airway swelling
Place the infant on continuous pulse oximetry and cardiorespiratory monitoring
Keep the head of the crib slightly raised

rationale.correct: Bronchiolitis care is supportive: suction, oxygen, hydration and monitoring; bronchodilators, steroids and antibiotics are not routine.

perOption.a: Infants breathe through the nose; clearing secretions improves breathing and feeding.
perOption.c: Bronchodilators are not routinely recommended for bronchiolitis.
perOption.d: Hydration support is needed when work of breathing interferes with feeding.
perOption.e: Steroids are not recommended for bronchiolitis.
perOption.g: Slight elevation can ease breathing and feeding.

references: Pediatric nursing texts (e.g. Hockenberry, Wong's Essentials of Pediatric Nursing)

questions.stem: Thirty minutes after oxygen is started, the infant's SpO2 is 93%, but the infant has stopped breathing for 20 seconds and the heart rate dropped to 82/min. What should the nurse do first?

options.text: Document the event and continue to watch the monitor closely for another episode
Gently stimulate the infant and be ready to give breaths with a bag-valve mask
Increase the oxygen flow and recheck the SpO2 in 5 minutes
Suction the mouth and nose deeply until the secretions are completely cleared

rationale.correct: Apnea with bradycardia in an infant needs stimulation and, if breathing does not resume, bag-valve-mask ventilation and a rapid response call.

perOption.a: Apnea with bradycardia needs immediate intervention, not observation alone.
perOption.b: Stimulation often restarts breathing; if not, the nurse gives positive-pressure breaths while calling for help.
perOption.c: Oxygen does not make an apneic infant breathe.
perOption.d: Deep, prolonged suctioning can worsen bradycardia; brief suction may help, but stimulation and breathing support come first.

questions.educationalObjective: Respond to apnea in an infant.

questions.stem: On day 3, the nurse reassesses the infant. For each finding, indicate whether it shows improvement or no improvement.

rows.text: Feeds for only 3 minutes before tiring and pulling away

rationale.correct: Lower work of breathing, normal oxygen saturation on room air and good urine output show recovery; adequate feeding is needed before discharge.

perOption.r1:c1: The rate is lower and work of breathing is less.
perOption.r4:c1: The infant still cannot feed well.
perOption.r4:c2: Poor feeding means the infant is not ready for discharge.

exhibits.title: Emergency department, 2200
exhibits.body: A 58-year-old client with alcohol-related cirrhosis vomited a large amount of bright red blood at home. The client is pale, anxious and restless. The abdomen is distended with ascites, and there are spider angiomas on the chest. Last alcohol drink was 2 days ago. Two large-bore IV catheters are in place.

exhibits.title: Pediatric unit, 0800
exhibits.body: A 3-month-old infant, born at 34 weeks, is admitted with 3 days of runny nose and cough and 1 day of poor feeding. The parent says the infant has had only 2 wet diapers since yesterday. The infant has thick nasal secretions, nasal flaring and subcostal retractions. Wheezes and crackles are heard in both lungs. A respiratory viral panel is positive for RSV.
